articles.summary: Mumbai: Vijay Singh, vice chairman of Tata Trusts and a trustee of the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT), has approached the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner seeking an immediate inquiry into the administration and governance of the charitable trust, including its involvement in the commercial and strategic affairs of Tata Sons."I have written to the charity commissioner around the same time as Venu Srinivasan, expressing similar concerns," Singh told ET.Also read: ET Exclusive: Venu Srinivasan seeks probe into Tata Trusts over alleged governance lapsesAs reported first by ET on September 30, Srinivasan, Tata Trusts vice chairman and its joint nominee director on the Tata Sons board, has sought an inquiry into the appointment and continued status of Noel Tata as a perpetual trustee and the basis on which he assumed and continues to hold the chairmanship of Tata Trusts. He has also sought scrutiny of the appointment of son Neville Tata as a trustee.Call for Action Singh also demanded inquiry into what he described as his (Srinivasan's) exclusion from relevant decision-making processes.Singh's submissions are on similar lines, including seeking an examination of the involvement of SDTT and its trustees in the commercial and strategic affairs of Tata Sons.He has raised concerns over the increasing involvement of SDTT and Tata Trusts in matters concerning Tata Sons."SDTT's substantial shareholding in Tata Sons cannot mean that the trust assumes the functions of a commercial enterprise or participates directly in Tata Sons' business affairs," Singh said in the letter to the charity commissioner.Singh also flagged potential tax implications arising from such involvement, citing provisions of the Income Tax Act, 2025, governing commercial activities by registered non-profit organisations. He has argued that activities not incidental to the trust's charitable objects could put its tax registration and exemption at risk."Given the substantial value of SDTT's shareholding in Tata Sons, the potential consequences for the trust and its charitable corpus could be immense," he has said.Also read: Tata companies face a tough call on Chandra vote at AGMThe two submissions - by Srinivasan and Singh - are now before the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner. On Wednesday, Tata Trusts made a submission to the charity commissioner asking to be heard before the official takes any decision on the complaints.Singh has sought consequential action based on the findings of the inquiry, including suspension or removal of trustees where warranted and appointment of trustees in accordance with the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act.He has also sought directions under Section 36A(1) of the Act restraining SDTT and its board from convening meetings, passing circular resolutions or undertaking processes relating to the administration, management or composition of the trust until completion of the inspector's inquiry. Singh has asked that pending an inquiry, status quo be maintained in relation to the composition of the SDTT board of trustees.His move comes amid widening differences within Tata Trusts over the functioning of SDTT and the role of its trustees in matters concerning Tata Sons.The development also comes against the backdrop of proceedings concerning SRTT. In May, Maharashtra Charity Commissioner Amogh S Kaloti directed SRTT's board to postpone its May 16 meeting and refrain from convening such meetings until the submission of an inspector's report, following complaints concerning the composition of the board and alleged non-compliance with Section 30A(2) of the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act.

The economy expanded 2.5% in the January-March quarter, the Associated Press reported.Growth in gross domestic product, which measures the output of goods and services, was supported by a sharp pickup in consumer spending and continued strength in business investment. Consumer spending, which accounts for about 70% of US economic activity, rose at a 3.8% annual rate in April-June, compared with 0.7% in the first quarter.The overall GDP figure was held back by a surge in imports. Imports rose at a 12.6% annual pace in the second quarter, partly driven by increased shipments of computer chips and other products supporting artificial intelligence investment. The jump in imports shaved nearly 1.7 percentage points off GDP growth.AI investment powers business spendingBusiness investment excluding housing rose at a 9% annual rate in the second quarter, reflecting continued spending linked to the artificial intelligence boom.A measure of underlying economic strength that excludes volatile government spending and trade expanded at a 4.6% rate, accelerating sharply from 1.8% in the first quarter.Housing investment also increased, rising 2.8% and recording its first increase since the end of 2024. The housing market has remained under pressure from elevated mortgage rates.The US economy has remained resilient despite fighting with Iran and the resulting spike in energy prices. The latest GDP estimate was the final of three Commerce Department readings for the second quarter, AP reported.The government’s first estimate of third-quarter GDP growth is due on October 29.

articles.title: Cabinet likely to raise wheat MSP by ₹25 to ₹2,610 per quintal for 2027-28
articles.summary:
The Union Cabinet is likely to have approved a Rs 25 per quintal increase in the minimum support price (MSP) of wheat, taking it to Rs 2,610 per quintal for the 2027-28 rabi marketing year, sources said on Wednesday.
The MSP for wheat for the 2026-27 marketing year (April-March) was fixed at Rs 2,585 per quintal.
Based on the recommendation of the Commission for Agricultural Costs & Prices (CACP), the agriculture ministry had proposed a nominal hike, factoring in the cost of production, El Nino concerns, and global and domestic price trends, the sources said.
The CACP's recommendation is believed to have been cleared at the Cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi earlier in the day, they added.
The agriculture ministry has set a wheat production target of 121 million tonnes for the 2026-27 crop year (July-June).
Wheat is the main rabi (winter) crop. Sowing usually begins in October, and harvesting starts in April.

articles.title: US H-1B lottery changes from Oct 1
articles.summary: The US is set to shift the selection method for H-1B visas toward more advantageous employment from October 1, 2026, giving more points to those with higher wages. The new system will be used in the FY2027 H-1B cap, and will be based on wages instead of an equal-weight lottery.The new system will allocate a number of registrations according to the salary requirements for the position being filled. Under the new system, H-1B registrations will receive a limited number of entries to the selection pool, depending on the salary requirement for the job being offered. Higher wage levels will receive more entries, increasing their chances of selection, while workers at the lowest wage level will remain eligible for the lottery.Also Read: Canada changes rules for foreign workers, bars staffing agencies from sponsoring work permitsThe change is particularly relevant for Indian professionals, who account for a large share of H-1B workers.How the new H-1B selection system worksThe amount of entries received into a registration will be dependent upon the highest US Department of Labor Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS) wage standard offered for a registering job's occupation and locale.Wage Level IV: Four entriesWage Level III: Three entriesWage Level II: Two entriesWage Level I: One entryThis means that the new system does not cut lower-paid jobs out of the H-1B lottery. Rather, it provides more representation for higher paid positions in the selection group.Also Read: From India to the US boardroom: Why L-1A is becoming a strategic US-expansion route for Indian mid-sized businessesThe Department of Homeland Security has estimated selection probabilities of about 15.29% for Level I, 30.58% for Level II, 45.87% for Level III and 61.16% for Level IV under the assumptions used in its analysis. USCIS has clarified that these figures are estimates and should not be treated as guaranteed selection rates.Salary details will matter moreThe wage information entered at the registration stage will become an important part of the H-1B process.If a registration is selected, the employer will need to provide evidence supporting the wage level claimed during registration. USCIS says details in the subsequent petition should generally match the registration, including the relevant Standard Occupational Classification (SOC) code and wage information.If the information does not match, the employer will have to explain the difference and submit supporting evidence. USCIS has warned that an inadequate explanation or lack of evidence could lead to the petition being rejected or denied.Multiple registrations face scrutinyUSCIS has also warned employers against submitting multiple or duplicate petitions for the same beneficiary.According to the agency, such filings could lead to denial or revocation, and filing fees may not be refunded.The agency will also count each unique beneficiary only once toward the H-1B numerical allocation, even if multiple registrations are submitted for that person.The new system applies to the FY2027 H-1B cap year, which starts on October 1, 2026.For FY2027 cap-subject petitions, the requested employment start date must be October 1, 2026, or later. USCIS generally does not allow these petitions to be filed more than six months before the requested start date.The annual H-1B cap itself remains unchanged at 65,000 visas, with another 20,000 slots for beneficiaries with a US master's degree or higher.For Indian professionals, the key change is that the H-1B lottery will no longer give every eligible registration the same weight. The wage level attached to the offered position will determine how many entries that registration gets in the selection pool.In effect, the FY2027 cycle moves the H-1B lottery from an equal-entry model to a system where the offered salary and corresponding wage level directly influence selection weight.

articles.title: Penguin in disguise: A new species found
articles.summary: Scientists have identified a new species of penguin for the first time in more than a century. The clue was not in how it looks. It was in its DNA.The bird is the southeastern gentoo penguin, named Pygoscelis kerguelensis. It lives on the sub-Antarctic Kerguelen Island and, most likely, nearby Heard Island in the southern Indian Ocean.Also read: 1,700-year-old Egyptian tomb contains a Greek poem, protective spells, Roman coins and ancient afterlife imageryOne species becomes fourFor years, the gentoo penguin was treated as a single species. It is found across Antarctica and on remote islands in the Southern Ocean.A new genetic study shows this is wrong. Over hundreds of thousands of years, gentoos split into four separate evolutionary lineages. Researchers say each one should be counted as its own species: the northern, southern, eastern and southeastern gentoo.Of the four, the southeastern gentoo was unknown to science until now.The southeastern gentoo looks just like the other gentoos. Scientists call this a "cryptic species". It is a species that looks the same on the outside but is clearly different in its genes.The team studied the whole genomes of 64 penguins from 10 breeding colonies. For the first time, the samples covered almost the entire range of the gentoo penguin. The findings were published in the journal Communications Biology.How the split happenedThe researchers say the gentoo's flexible diet played a role. Gentoos eat a wide range of food, so different groups settled in very different places. Over time, each group adapted to its own environment. The southeastern gentoo evolved close to the Polar Front, the zone where cold Antarctic waters meet warmer waters to the north.A long debate endsGentoo taxonomy has been argued over for years. Some researchers had earlier suggested splitting the bird into as many as six species. A 2020 study proposed four. The new paper is a consensus of experts from several countries, backed by much larger genetic data."There's probably no species of penguin where the taxonomy has been more debated than the gentoo penguin," said Rauri Bowie, a professor at the University of California, Berkeley, and a co-senior author of the study.Why it mattersThe new count changes how the birds are protected. Earlier, a healthy gentoo population in one region could hide the decline of another. Now each species can be assessed on its own.Three of the four are already considered threatened as climate change alters the Antarctic and sub-Antarctic. The southern gentoo, the only one living in Antarctica itself, faces less climate risk and may even expand its range. The southeastern gentoo has a small population and is among those whose future is uncertain.Also read: Why NASA is studying 1.2-billion-year-old Scottish rocks for clues to ancient life on Mars and the Red Planet’s watery pastBowie told The Washington Post that the study also showed how urgently these fragile ecosystems need protection. The researchers want conservation bodies in every country involved to recognise the new species and act to save them.The team says the genetic data will have other uses. One researcher is already searching the penguin genomes for changes that help birds survive avian influenza, which is hitting penguins, other birds and mammals across the world.The gentoo is the third-largest penguin, after the emperor and the king.
